title: Breaking and Entering: Now or Never with Elise Peyronnet
transcript:
Elise Peyronnet, Artistic Director of Now or Never, joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studio to discuss the festival's 2026 program. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 2 July 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: The Artistic Director of the festival, Elise Peyronnet, is with me in the studio. Hey, Elise.

Elise: Hi, Lauren.

Lauren: Lovely to catch up with you again. You and I go way back, to your Melbourne Music Week days, many, many moons ago.

Elise: That's true, actually. We've known each other for a little while. But thank you so much for having me today.

Lauren: It's an incredible line-up you've put together for the fourth year of the festival, which was born from Melbourne Music Week and Melbourne Knowledge Week combining forces, and is now the City of Melbourne's annual festival of art, ideas, sound and technology. This year's curatorial theme is A Whole New World. What's your vision as Artistic Director, and how does that theme shape the program?

Elise: Well, the theme was chosen many, many months ago, and as the world unfolded, looking at everything that's happening geopolitically, we are absolutely in a whole new world. But initially, the theme was really talking to the technological shifts we're seeing in our everyday lives. Of course, we talk a lot about AI, and we're only just starting to see its impact. So we wanted a theme broad enough to really discuss that, maybe not necessarily fearing it, but just acknowledging that we are indeed in a whole new world.

For a curatorial theme, it's interesting to cover that in the talks. But in terms of creating events, too, there are a lot of events around the city where we're going to take over buildings and change the experience people have of different areas of the city. That's also inviting the audience to step into a whole new world.

Lauren: Technology is one of the festival's core pillars, so I imagine your curatorial and programming teams are having some big conversations about AI, with the ways we understand knowledge seemingly being reshaped at the moment. How have you been navigating that shift, and how is it reflected in the program?

Elise: Yes, it's a current theme, and one that I think we're still grappling with. It's a really hot topic for artists as well. We've discussed it since the beginning of Now or Never. In fact, Now or Never was created in 2023, so already in 2022 it was really the beginning of AI in everyday life. So it's always been a core topic. We question it, but it is here. Probably all of us use it every day. But it is scary when it's brought to light in an artistic sense: does it really replace human agency and artistic expression or not, or is it just a tool that can enhance them? We're still at the beginning of that conversation.

Lauren: There are a few events in the program that reflect on that. The festival runs across 12 days, with more than 250 local and international artists and creatives and over 150 events. Where do you start putting a program like this together? Was there a particular moment that locked in first?

Elise: It always comes from the venues, the locations. Since the beginning, we've worked on creating really unique experiences at the Royal Exhibition Building, so that was one of the concepts we started to work on, but it took a really long time to come to fruition. So again, spaces: looking at the city and where we want to place things. For me, it always starts there.

Lauren: Now or Never has a reputation for commissioning really unique site-specific work. I imagine there are creative challenges in programming cutting-edge technology events inside buildings that are centuries old, like the Royal Exhibition Building and Melbourne Town Hall. What sort of challenges have you faced?

Elise: In fact, every year is a different one. This year it's a completely different take on the Royal Exhibition Building. We're bringing back a series of music, a series of really slow-paced, meditative shows that are almost the counterpart of technology, in a way. If anything, it's about slowing down and being in the moment, and I think that was an interesting balance to have in the program. So in a way we're going without technology — or not without technology, but really thinking about being in the present, and experiencing music in a different way.

Lauren: Speaking of slowing down, there's an event that slows down so much it's a mass slumber party: you can sleep over at the Royal Exhibition Building, at an event called Somnia, which sounds pretty incredible. Can you talk us through it?

Elise: Yes, this is quite a unique experience, where we invite the audience to come and take a bed. At the Royal Exhibition Building, we'll have a durational concert with multiple artists. First we have Bendik Giske, an amazing saxophonist and experimental artist, who has worked with Caterina Barbieri and really reinvented the saxophone as an instrument. It's quite a physical experience: you can hear him breathe through the instrument. That's the first part of the night.

After that, we've invited William Basinski, the amazing American experimental composer, to perform continuously the series of four albums he created, The Disintegration Loops, which are a landmark ambient work for a lot of music lovers. We were really looking for a piece of music that could have that pace, inviting reflection and meditation. The music is quite melancholic. It's actually about disappearing. It came from digitising the tapes of music he had created: as they played, the loops were disappearing, and the music was disappearing. So it's a very profound piece of music. It will go for six hours. You can decide to stay up, move around the venue, or take the bed and just stay there.

Lauren: And when you say take the bed, people don't have to bring their own bed.

Elise: Sorry. Take the bed you've been assigned. Then we'll have a wake-up moment, and a little breakfast, before people leave the venue.

Lauren: That sounds incredible. I actually listened to the whole of — or one of the tracks of William Basinski's The Disintegration Loops last night, in preparation for this interview. It's believed to have influenced many artists, including Burial. What do you need to consider to support the audience through such an intense sonic experience over those 10 hours?

Elise: We just want to give the audience some comfort. I think it's important. I think you experience music in a completely different way when you are lying down. It's also linked, maybe, to the deep listening experiences that are really blossoming everywhere. There are a lot more at the moment, because maybe people are looking for a different way of taking in music. That's what we're trying to emulate: to create an environment that will be conducive to this.

Lauren: Is it a work you'd experienced yourself before bringing it to Melbourne?

Elise: No, no. I've always wanted to do a sleep event. Of course, we looked at Max Richter, who has performed in Australia before. But this was curated especially for Melbourne, with Melbourne in mind. And yes, it's the first of maybe many. We'll see how we go this year.

Lauren: I'm sure you'd advise people to rug up as well, given it's the middle of winter in Melbourne.

Elise: Yes, yes. It's BYO for the bedding.

Lauren: For fans of Philip Glass, there's an homage to the world-renowned American composer as part of the festival as well. Can you tell us about that event?

Elise: Again, this has been curated as part of a full series around that meditative state. Philip Glass's music is that beautiful, repetitive, minimalist music, and he has influenced so many composers in so many genres. When we program music, we're always looking to bring some diversity, and not just electronic-based music. We're an art and technology festival, but innovation and experimentation are really the key driving factors for us in programming some of these acts.

I really wanted to bring that music, which is usually presented in concert halls, into a different environment: the Royal Exhibition Building, with the stage in the centre, under the dome, and the audience seated around it. And I wanted it to be accessible to as many people as possible who might want to discover that music. First we have Orchestra Victoria, close to 30 musicians on stage, performing a piece by Philip Glass that's rarely performed alone; it's initially a ballet piece. Then we have Maki Namekawa, a fantastic pianist and soloist who has worked and collaborated with Philip Glass. She's going to perform the piano Etudes one to 10, which are really landmark piano works. And piano is very accessible. It's going to be a really beautiful night.

Lauren: Gorgeous. Elise, there's also a headline late-night music program at Melbourne Town Hall, with a whole bunch of local and international artists across three nights. Can you take us through what's happening there?

Elise: Yes. Town Hall is going to be transformed for the full duration of the festival, taking different shapes. First we have Robin Fox, with a new commissioned piece that's going to take over the main hall: an installation, lots of lasers, all around the room. That runs during the week, free for the public. We've also invited Chunky Move to present a new dance work inside Town Hall. So that's how the festival starts.

Then, as we move into the second weekend, we change the venue over into more of a music venue, with three nights, two of them with local promoters. We really wanted to do that in the spirit of Melbourne Music Week, and how we've worked in the past with lots of the amazing independent promoters we have here in Melbourne. We've invited Chuleo Club, who are amazing, promoting Latinx, Latin club, underground music, and have been doing that for many years, mainly at Miscellania. We really wanted to profile them and work with them. They've curated an amazing line-up. We have A.Chal, we have Dinamarca, some artists who have actually never played in Melbourne before, so we're very excited about that. And Zalina, who is the head honcho, I guess, of Chuleo Club, will also be performing.

On the Saturday we have Octave One, the legendary Detroit producers, playing live. It's a really great live show, very big and fun to watch, and in fact the entire night is built around artists playing with hardware. So we have Sleep D as well, and Hybrid Man, who's going to come and perform that night, and JNETT as well. And to close on the Sunday, we're bringing back My Disco, who I think haven't been performing for many years. So it's kind of their return with us. We're very excited to have them back.

Lauren: What did you say to My Disco to get them to reform for you?

Elise: I think it was just the right time, apparently. I think they were ready. They wanted to. It didn't really take that much, I don't know…

Lauren: Convincing.

Elise: Convincing, maybe. And maybe what helped as well was that we knew we had Robin Fox closing too, and they're close in their relationships and artistic endeavours. So I would say it's Robin who influenced their decision.

Lauren: There's also Derrick Gee's Radio Hour; Derrick's been a guest on this program before. His show is all about deep listening, and Melbourne Recital Centre, with that acoustically treated room, is going to be the perfect venue for it. What's the concept for that show, and what can audiences expect?

Elise: I agree that the venue is going to lend itself really well. It's really intimate. It's like an old-school radio show, in a way. Derrick Gee, for those who don't know him, is an internet personality. He has interviewed amazing artists, international big names and smaller names, and he's just really good at explaining music to anyone, really. He really embodies what a music critic could be, but in a really conversational way. So he has put together his night. He's inviting Julia Jacklin, who's going to be chatting with him, performing, playing some tracks, and Michael Kucyk, who is the boss of Efficient Space, an amazing label as well. So it's a really great night of chats in a living-room environment.

Lauren: Very cool. As a bit of a disclaimer, through my work as a programmer at the Wheeler Centre, I've been involved in putting the talks program together with your team at Now or Never. But there was one I wanted to mention in particular, because it features speakers who are very near and dear to many RRR listeners: Sosefina Fuamoli, Sarah Smith, and Al Newstead, who's recently written a book on Tame Impala's Currents for the 33⅓ series, hosted by a good friend of this show, Simon Winkler, who of course was the co-host of Breaking and Entering for 18 years. They're coming together at the Wheeler Centre for what should be a really fascinating conversation on music criticism. There's so much to discover as part of Now or Never, including some incredible large-scale light installations along the Birrarung/Yarra River. Is there anything else you'd like to draw our attention to, some of your other favourites?

Elise: I hope there are different layers, different ways of interacting with Now or Never. We have a really large program of free, amazing installations all around the city. You mentioned Southbank, and we have some projections onto Hamer Hall. We have an amazing artist, AKA Chang from Taiwan, who's coming for the first time, presenting a laser installation on the river, reflecting onto the water. We have Emily Parsons-Lord, an amazing Melbourne-based artist, who's going to make the Evan Walker Bridge disappear in mist. So there'll be lots of really large-scale installations around there. And if you start from Melbourne Town Hall with Robin Fox, you'll be able to have a full experience of the city all lit up, and really see amazing artists, and some really great local talent, on a bigger scale.

Lauren: Incredible. Congratulations, Elise, on another amazing program. Now or Never takes over the city from 19 to 30 August. Thanks so much, Elise.

Elise: Thank you, Lauren.
